questions.content: The diameter of small Nerf balls is approximately normal with mean 5.2 inches and standard deviation 0.08 inches. For a random sample of 20 balls, find the interval containing the central 95.44% of sample means.

questions.content:
A population has mean $\mu=20$ and standard deviation $\sigma=4$. A random sample of 64 measurements is selected.

a. Describe the shape of the sampling distribution of $\bar X$ and state whether the population must be normal.

b. Find its mean and standard deviation.

c. Find $P(\bar X>21)$.

d. Find $P(\bar X<19.385)$.
questions.source: Assigments for Speaking of Statistics-Semester1-2014-2015/Assignment and solution_chap7&13_ Sampling distribution_regression.docx

questions.content: The number of flaws per flash drive has probabilities $P(X=0)=0.65$, $P(X=1)=0.20$, $P(X=2)=0.10$, and $P(X=3)=0.05$. A random sample of 100 drives is rejected when its mean number of flaws exceeds 0.75. The population mean is 0.55. Find the approximate probability that a shipment is rejected.
questions.source: Assigments for Speaking of Statistics-Semester1-2014-2015/Assignment and solution_chap7&13_ Sampling distribution_regression.docx

questions.content:
Historically, 48% of Bank of America customers express customer delight. In a random sample of 350 customers, 189 (54%) express delight.

a. Assuming $p=0.48$, find the approximate probability of observing a sample proportion at least 0.54.

b. Assess the claim that the current proportion exceeds 48%.
questions.source: Assigments for Speaking of Statistics-Semester1-2014-2015/Assignment and solution_chap7&13_ Sampling distribution_regression.docx

questions.content: A poll of 900 voters predicts that 55% support the incumbent governor. Assume the true support is $p=0.51$. Find the approximate probability of observing a sample proportion of at least 0.55.
questions.source: Assigments for Speaking of Statistics-Semester1-2014-2015/Assignment and solution_chap7&13_ Sampling distribution_regression.docx

questions.content: The amount dispensed by a soft-drink machine is normal with mean 7 ounces and standard deviation 0.5 ounce. For samples of 9 cups, find the value exceeded by 95% of the sample means.

The population of annual absence days is $1,3,6,7,7,12$. Sampling is without replacement.

a. List all 20 samples of size 3 and give the sampling distribution of $\bar X$.

b. Find the mean of the sample means and compare it with the population mean.

E-mail session time is normal with mean 8 minutes and standard deviation 2 minutes.

a. For $n=25$, find $\operatorname{SD}(\bar X)$.

b. For $n=25$, find $P(7.8<\bar X<8.2)$.

c. For $n=100$, find the same probability.

d. Explain the difference.
\ne. Compare the likelihoods of one session exceeding 11 minutes, a 25-session mean exceeding 9 minutes, and a 100-session mean exceeding 8.6 minutes.

Bank-teller service time has mean 3.10 minutes and standard deviation 0.40 minute. For a random sample of 16 customers:

a. Find $P(\bar X\ge3)$.

b. Find $k$ such that $P(\bar X<k)=0.85$.

c. State the distributional assumption needed.

Annual distance traveled per truck is normal with mean 50.0 thousand miles and standard deviation 12.0 thousand miles. For a sample of 64 trucks:

a. Find the 95th percentile of the sample mean.

b. What assumption is needed?

Historically, 70% of people are classified as successful. In a random sample of 64 people, 48 are successful. Find the sample proportion and the standard error of the sample proportion using the historical value $p=0.70$.

Thirty percent of credit-card purchases exceed $\$100. For random samples of 100 purchases:

a. Find the proportion of samples with 20% to 30% over $\$100$.

b. Find symmetric limits around 30% containing 95% of sample proportions.

Students guess which of two soft drinks they taste, so the correct-identification probability is $p=0.50$. For samples of 200 students:

a. Find the proportion of samples with 50% to 60% correct.

b. Find symmetric limits containing 90% of sample proportions.

c. Find $P(\hat p>0.65)$.

d. Compare $P(\hat p>0.60)$ for $n=200$ with $P(\hat p>0.55)$ for $n=1000$.
Why is it useful to calculate a confidence interval in addition to a point estimate of a population parameter?
As the degrees of freedom of a Student's $t$ distribution increase, how do (a) its standard deviation and (b) its critical values $t_{\alpha}$ and $t_{\alpha/2}$ change?
When is a one-sample $t$ confidence interval appropriate for estimating a population mean $\mu$?

For 65 customer satisfaction ratings, the sample mean is $\bar x=42.95$ and the known population standard deviation is $\sigma=2.64$.

a. Calculate 95% and 99% confidence intervals for $\mu$.

b. Can we be 95% confident that $\mu\ge42$?

c. Can we be 99% confident that $\mu\ge42$?

d. Interpret the results.
A preliminary sample gives $s=32.866$ dollars per square foot. How large a sample is needed for 95% confidence that the sample mean is within $\$10$ of the population mean?

For 49 midsize cars, the sample mean mileage is $31.5531$ mpg. Assume the population standard deviation is $0.8$ mpg. Test $H_0:\mu\le31$ against $H_a:\mu>31$ at $\alpha=0.05$, and report the p-value. Would the decision change at $\alpha=0.01$?
Credit-card interest rates for nine cards are 16.7, 17.4, 17.0, 17.8, 15.4, 13.1, 15.8, 14.3, and 14.5 percent. Test $H_0:\mu=14$ against $H_a:\mu>14$ at $\alpha=0.01$.
Nationally, 20% of condominium renters move in a year. In a random sample of 200 Dallas-area renters, 56 moved. Test $H_0:p=0.20$ against $H_a:p>0.20$ at $\alpha=0.10$ and find the p-value.

Canned-tuna weight is normal with mean 5.95 ounces and standard deviation 0.2 ounces. The sample size increases from 42 to 84.

a. How does the standard deviation of $\bar X$ change?

b. How does $E(\bar X)$ change?

c. Is the Central Limit Theorem needed for normality of $\bar X$?
